guide.title: Onboarding & Installfest (Welcome Aboard, Prep Machine + CLI, Interacting with Assignments)
guide.summary: Day 1 turns your Mac into a developer machine: terminal basics, Homebrew, Python, Node, Git, the GitHub CLI, PostgreSQL, Docker and VS Code. It ends with the fork, clone, commit, push loop you use for every assignment.
guide.goal: Run Python, JavaScript and SQL from your terminal, and fork, clone, commit and push a Code Platoon assignment.
required: Installfest assignment: CLI Practice (the Terminal Tutor course, then the local test/ folder exercise)
Installfest goal (TLO): run Python, JS and SQL programs from the command line and install dependencies with pip and npm
Installfest goal (TLO): write and edit code with VS Code
Installfest skill (ELO): use git on the command line, logged in to your GitHub account, to clone repos and push code
Interacting with Assignments: fork the assignment, work on it locally or in Codespaces, run its tests, then commit and push to your fork (no pull request needed)

steps.title: Install Docker Desktop and VS Code
steps.detail: Your CLAUDE.md already lists Docker and VS Code on this Mac, so this is a check, not a fresh install. In VS Code, open the command palette (Cmd+Shift+P) and run "Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH" so `code` works from any terminal.
steps.code: docker --version
steps.doneWhen: docker --version prints a version, and typing `code .` in a terminal opens that folder in VS Code.

steps.title: Install Homebrew and check its health
steps.detail: Homebrew is the Mac's package manager: it installs and updates developer tools for you. Install it from brew.sh if `brew` isn't found, then update it and run the health check.
steps.code:
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
brew update
brew doctor
steps.doneWhen: brew doctor says "Your system is ready to brew." Warnings are OK to read and skip for now.

steps.title: Install Python and a default venv
steps.detail: A virtual environment (venv) keeps each project's Python packages separate. Your CLAUDE.md lists Python 3.14, so just confirm it, then create and activate the default venv. Heads-up: the page creates `~/.default`, but its starter .zshrc line says `source $HOME/default/bin/activate` (no dot). Use the same name in both places or new terminals will show an error.
steps.code:
python3 --version
brew install python
cd ~
python3 -m venv .default
source ~/.default/bin/activate
steps.doneWhen: You see (.default) at the start of your prompt, and `deactivate` removes it.

steps.title: Install Node.js and npm
steps.detail: Node runs JavaScript outside the browser; npm installs JavaScript packages. Your CLAUDE.md lists Node 26, so the version checks are the important part.
steps.code:
brew install npm
sudo npm install -g n
sudo n stable
node -v
npm -v
steps.doneWhen: node -v and npm -v both print version numbers.

steps.title: Configure Git and log in to GitHub
steps.detail: Git saves snapshots of your code on your machine; GitHub stores them online. Use your GitHub username (cruzjay188) and the email on your GitHub account. You're already logged in to `gh` as cruzjay188, so the clone test just proves it works.
steps.code:
git config --global user.name "<YOUR_NAME>"
git config --global user.email "<YOUR_EMAIL>"
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
git config --global -l
gh auth login
gh repo clone lodash/lodash
rm -rf lodash
steps.doneWhen: git config --global -l shows your user.name, user.email and core.editor=code --wait, and the lodash clone works.

steps.title: Install PostgreSQL and open psql
steps.detail: PostgreSQL is the database the course uses later (Supabase runs it in the cloud). Your CLAUDE.md doesn't list Postgres, so check whether you did this on Day 1.
steps.code:
brew install postgresql@14
brew services restart postgresql@14
psql postgres
steps.doneWhen: Your prompt changes to postgres=#. Type \q to leave.

steps.title: Add Live Server to VS Code
steps.detail: Every Knowledge Check is a team quiz you open with Live Server (right-click index.html → Open with Live Server). It's in the Installfest's recommended extensions, along with ESLint, Prettier, GitLens and others.
steps.doneWhen: Right-clicking an index.html in VS Code shows "Open with Live Server".

steps.title: Practice the command line (CLI Practice)
steps.detail: Do the Terminal Tutor course, then the README's exercise on your own Mac: make a test folder in ~, make test.txt with touch, edit it with `code`, view it with head/tail/less, go up a level and delete the folder. progress.md shows cli-practice as done, so use the README's "Points to Ponder" (cd ., cd .., cd ~, cd /, making, renaming and deleting files) as a self-quiz.
steps.doneWhen: You can answer every Points to Ponder question without looking it up.

steps.title: Learn the fork, clone, commit, push loop
steps.detail: Fork the assignment on GitHub (your own copy), clone your fork, work, then commit and push. In this workspace `/start-assignment` and `/save-project` do this for you, but know the manual commands too. Assignments aren't graded, and you submit by pushing.
steps.code:
git clone https://github.com/your-username/assignment-name.git
cd assignment-name
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Complete assignment section 1"
git push origin main
steps.doneWhen: Your commit shows on your fork's GitHub page (for example github.com/cruzjay188/cli-practice).

The family of operating systems macOS and Linux come from, which is why they share commands like ls and cd.

A folder that holds one project's Python packages so projects don't clash.
A settings file your terminal runs every time it opens, used for PATH changes and aliases.

guide.title: Intro to Full Stack Dev
guide.summary: A concepts-only lesson on how a web app works end to end: the front-end, back-end, database and infrastructure layers, and how a request travels from the browser to a server and back (IP, TCP, DNS, HTTP, AJAX, JSON).
guide.goal: Trace a user action from the screen to the database and back, naming the HTTP method and status code at each step.
required: Part I: Knowledge Check 1 – Intro to Full Stack (team quiz, FS-Knowledge-Check-1)
Part II: Knowledge Check 2 – Full Stack Development Breakdown (team quiz, fs-knowledge-check-2)

steps.title: Read Full Stack Workflow
steps.detail: Read the lecture's four layers (front-end, back-end, database, infrastructure) and its "You Open Instagram" walkthrough. The point is a mental model, not code.
steps.doneWhen: You can say in one sentence what each of the four layers is responsible for.

steps.title: Learn the web vocabulary
steps.detail: IP is WHERE a server is, TCP is HOW the bytes get there reliably, HTTP is WHAT the message says, and AJAX lets a page send requests without reloading. Knowledge Check 1 also covers DNS and JSON. Write one line on each in a topic note such as notes/topics/how-the-web-works.md.
steps.doneWhen: Your note explains IP, TCP, DNS, HTTP, AJAX and JSON in your own words.

steps.title: Take Knowledge Check 1 with your team
steps.detail: Open assignments/week-01/FS-Knowledge-Check-1 in VS Code, right-click index.html → Open with Live Server. After each question, discuss why the answer is right or wrong. progress.md shows this done; retake it alone to see what stuck.
steps.doneWhen: You finished the quiz and can explain the reasoning behind any answer you missed.

steps.title: Read Full Stack Breakdown
steps.detail: This lecture covers the HTTP conversation, front-end components that depend on data, and the back-end's job of validating and serializing data. Keep its "Rinse and Repeat" cycle in mind: request, response, UI update.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain why HTTP is called stateless and what serialization means.

steps.title: Map CRUD to HTTP methods and status codes
steps.detail: Make a small table in your topic note: each CRUD action, its HTTP method, and the status codes you'd expect. You'll use this exact mapping in AI-7, when you send requests to Supabase from Postman.
steps.code:
Create → POST
Read   → GET
Update → PUT / PATCH
Delete → DELETE
steps.doneWhen: Your table lists all four actions plus what 2xx, 4xx and 5xx codes mean.

steps.title: Take Knowledge Check 2 with your team
steps.detail: Same Live Server routine in assignments/week-01/fs-knowledge-check-2. It covers HTTP methods and status codes, CRUD, serialization, and front-end vs back-end jobs.
steps.doneWhen: Quiz finished, and you discussed every answer you got wrong.

steps.title: Diagram one request in your Netflix clone
steps.detail: The lesson's assignments are conceptual: you should be able to diagram a request flow. Pick one action in Myflix (assignments/week-02/netflix), such as adding a title to My List, and draw it through all the layers in TLDraw or a Mermaid diagram in your notes.
steps.doneWhen: Your diagram shows browser → request (method) → Supabase → table → response (status code) → UI update.

concepts.meaning: Understanding every layer of an app (UI, server logic, data and hosting) and how they talk to each other.
The part users see and click, running in the browser.
The server code that applies business rules, validates data and talks to the database.
IP finds where a server is; TCP delivers the data there reliably and in order.
The internet's phone book: it turns a name like netflix.com into an IP address.
The format for web requests and responses; it's stateless, so every request stands on its own.
Sending a request from JavaScript in the background so the page updates without a full reload.
A text format for data ({"key": "value"}) that front-ends and back-ends send to each other.
Create, Read, Update, Delete: the four things almost every app does with data.
The number in a response that tells you what happened: 2xx worked, 4xx your request was wrong, 5xx the server broke.
Turning data into a format like JSON so it can travel over the network.

guide.title: Working with LLMs
guide.summary: How large language models produce text (next-token prediction, Transformers, attention), and how to write prompts that reliably get useful answers using the CREF framework and named prompting techniques.
guide.goal: Write a structured prompt with CREF and work out whether a bad answer came from your prompt or from the model's limits.
required: Part I: IBM – Getting Started with Generative AI
Part I: Anthropic – AI Fluency for Students
Part I: Anthropic – AI Capabilities & Limitations
Part I: FreeCodeCamp Python Certification – complete 50 steps
Part II: IBM – Craft Precise Prompts for AI Models
Part II: FreeCodeCamp JavaScript Certification – complete 100 steps

steps.title: Read "What are Large Language Models"
steps.detail: Follow the path from rule-based to retrieval-based to generative chatbots, then how an LLM predicts the next token. Note which models are encoder-only, decoder-only or encoder-decoder, and how Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT compare.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain next-token prediction to a friend in two sentences.

steps.title: Learn CREF and the five bad-prompt patterns
steps.detail: CREF stands for Clarity, Role/Context, Examples, Format. The five failure patterns are too vague, missing context, contradictory, overloaded and assumed knowledge. Study the lecture's "Anatomy of a Good Prompt".
steps.code:
[Role / Persona]
You are a software engineering instructor teaching junior developers.

[Context]
The student just learned about for loops in Python and is now seeing list 
comprehensions for the first time.

[Task]
Explain list comprehensions step by step, starting from the equivalent for loop,
and then showing the compressed syntax.

[Format]
Use a code block for each example. Keep the explanation under 200 words.

[Constraint]
Do not use lambda functions or any concepts beyond basic iteration.
steps.doneWhen: You can take a vague prompt like "Help me with my code" and rewrite it to fix each CREF gap.

steps.title: Run the iterative prompting experiment
steps.detail: Open Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini in three tabs. Work through Scenario 1's six prompts in order in one conversation, then Scenario 2 (Resume Review). After each answer, note what the model assumed and what was missing. The first two prompts are below; the rest are on the page.
steps.code:
Help me plan a birthday party.

Plan a birthday party for my 8-year-old daughter. There will be 15 kids.
Our budget is $200.
steps.doneWhen: You have a short note on which refinement changed the answer most, and which model did best at each stage.

steps.title: Try the four named techniques
steps.detail: Zero-shot (no examples), few-shot (2–3 examples first), chain-of-thought (reason step by step) and role/persona. Try the lecture's chain-of-thought example, then write one of each for something from your own week.
steps.code:
A Django view is returning a 500 error when a POST request comes in but works fine
for GET requests. Think through the most likely causes step by step, then suggest
a debugging strategy.
steps.doneWhen: You've written and tested one prompt for each technique.

steps.title: Diagnose a bad response
steps.detail: Ask "whose fault is it?" A prompt problem (too general, missed the point, inconsistent) is fixed by rewording. A model limit (hallucination, knowledge cutoff, context window, capability ceiling) needs a different approach, like pasting in current docs. If three rewrites fail the same way, it's probably the model.
steps.doneWhen: You can name the four model limitations and what to do about each.

steps.title: Part I: IBM and Anthropic courses
steps.detail: Do IBM's Getting Started with Generative AI, then Anthropic's AI Fluency for Students and AI Capabilities & Limitations. The page warns that AI changes fast, so some course content may be outdated. These aren't tracked in progress.md, so keep your own checklist.
steps.doneWhen: All three courses show as completed in their platforms.

steps.title: Part I: 50 FreeCodeCamp Python steps
steps.detail: Complete 50 steps of the FreeCodeCamp Python certification.
steps.doneWhen: Your FreeCodeCamp progress shows 50 more Python steps done.

steps.title: Part II: precise prompts + 100 JavaScript steps
steps.detail: Do IBM's Craft Precise Prompts for AI Models, then 100 steps of the FreeCodeCamp JavaScript certification. (The page's JavaScript line says "for receiving your Python Certification", which looks like a typo; the link goes to JavaScript.)
steps.doneWhen: The IBM course is complete and FreeCodeCamp shows 100 more JavaScript steps.

concepts.meaning: A model trained on huge amounts of text that writes by predicting the next token over and over.
The model picks the most likely next piece of text, adds it, and repeats.
The model design that lets an LLM weigh every part of the conversation at once when choosing the next token.
Shaping what you give a model, on purpose, so its answers are accurate and in the format you need.
Clarity, Role/Context, Examples, Format: four checks for a good prompt.
Asking with no examples vs. showing 2–3 input → output examples first.
Asking the model to reason step by step before answering, which helps with debugging and math.
A confident, plausible answer that is simply wrong.
The date the model's training data ends; it doesn't know anything newer unless you paste it in.

guide.title: Coding Assistants
guide.summary: A coding agent is an LLM inside a loop that can use tools (read files, run commands) connected through MCP. You then install Claude Code and learn to pick a model, effort level and output style with cost in mind.
guide.goal: Set up Claude Code (Sonnet, Low effort, Default output style, voice, status line) and explain the agent loop and MCP.
required: Part I: Knowledge Check 3 – Intro to Coding Agents (team quiz)
Part I: Get caught up – make sure all assignments from previous lectures are done
Part I: FreeCodeCamp Python Certification – complete 50 steps
Part II: Knowledge Check 4 – Installing Claude Code (team quiz)
Part II: Claude Code Preparation Checklist (claude-code-checklist)
Part II: Get caught up – make sure all assignments from previous lectures are done
Part II: FreeCodeCamp JavaScript Certification – complete 100 steps

steps.title: Read Intro to Coding Agents
steps.detail: A coding agent wraps an LLM in a loop: build context, ask the LLM, run any tool call it returns, feed the result back, and repeat until the LLM answers with plain text. Learn its four parts (the agent, MCP, tools, the LLM) and why swapping the LLM doesn't change the loop.
steps.doneWhen: You can draw the agent loop from task to final answer and say what MCP standardizes ("USB for AI tools").

steps.title: Install Claude Code and log in
steps.detail: Checklist items 1–3. You already use Claude Code, so this is the verify pass: open a new terminal, check the version, then check your account inside Claude.
steps.code:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
claude --version
claude
/status
steps.doneWhen: claude --version prints a version, /status shows your account, and relaunching asks for no setup screens.

steps.title: Make Sonnet your default model
steps.detail: Checklist item 4. In the /model picker, press Enter to save it as the default (pressing s only changes this session). Know the other aliases too: Opus or Fable for hard problems, Haiku for quick lookups, and opusplan, which plans with Opus and then builds with Sonnet.
steps.code: /model sonnet
steps.doneWhen: After relaunching `claude`, the model shown is Sonnet.

steps.title: Set effort Low and output style Default
steps.detail: Checklist items 5–6. Higher effort means more tool calls and more tokens, so it costs more. The checklist wants Low as your default; raise it on purpose for hard tasks, then set it back. For output style, run /config, arrow to output-style and pick Default (Learning mode explains more if you want it later).
steps.code: /config
steps.doneWhen: After a relaunch, effort is still Low and /config shows output-style = Default.

steps.title: Turn on voice and build a status line
steps.detail: Checklist items 7–8. Run /voice, then hold the spacebar to talk and release to transcribe. Then paste the checklist's example status line prompt, which shows repo, branch, context use, cost and model under your prompt.
steps.code:
/voice
/statusline single line, fully color-coded with truecolor RGB gradient: repo name bold yellow, 🌿 leaf icon + git branch in bold cyan with parentheses, 20-block context bar using 24-bit RGB gradient from green(0,200,80) through yellow(220,200,0) to red(220,40,20) with dark gray(60,60,60) empty blocks, dynamic emoji that changes with usage (🟢 under 20%, ⚡ 20-69%, 🔥 70-89%, 🚨 90%+), percentage colored by usage level, session cost in yellow, code velocity showing +lines in green and -lines in red, 🤖 robot icon + model name in magenta, dim gray pipe separators between all elements
steps.doneWhen: Holding the spacebar transcribes your speech, and a status line shows repo, branch, a context bar, cost and model.

steps.title: Understand tokens and cost
steps.detail: A token is about 4 characters (about ¾ of a word). Every turn resends the whole conversation, so long chats cost more. Prompt caching and the Batch API (50% off) bring that down. Compare the lecture's price table (per million tokens): Fable $10/$50, Opus $4/$20, Sonnet $2/$10, Haiku $1/$5.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain why a long session costs more than a short one, and when you'd pick Haiku, Sonnet, Opus or Fable.

steps.title: Take Knowledge Checks 3 and 4
steps.detail: Team quizzes with Live Server: assignments/week-01/Knowledge-Check-3-Intro-to-Coding-Agents (agent loop, MCP, tool categories, Claude Code vs Cursor vs Copilot) and Knowledge-Check-4-Installing-Claude-Code (aliases and pricing, context and tokens, effort, output styles, Batch API, local models). progress.md shows both done.
steps.doneWhen: Both quizzes finished, and you can explain any answer you missed.

steps.title: Optional: run a free local model
steps.detail: Optional checklist item 9. Don't do this during class: it's a big download and uses a lot of RAM and CPU. Check you have at least 8 GB of RAM (16 GB recommended) and 4 GB of free disk. Suggested models: qwen3-coder, devstral, deepseek-r1, llama3.1.
steps.code:
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
ollama --version
ollama launch claude --model <model name>
steps.doneWhen: ollama --version prints a version (or you've decided to skip this optional item).

steps.title: Tick the checklist and do FreeCodeCamp
steps.detail: progress.md lists claude-code-checklist as "verify all boxes done", so walk its Final Check list from top to bottom. Then do 50 Python steps (Part I) and 100 JavaScript steps (Part II) on FreeCodeCamp.
steps.doneWhen: Every required Final Check box is ticked, and FreeCodeCamp shows the new Python and JavaScript steps.

concepts.meaning: Software that wraps an LLM in a loop with tools, so it can read files, run commands and edit code until the task is done.
Ask the LLM, run the tool it requests, feed back the result, and repeat until it answers with plain text.
An open standard for plugging tools into AI agents: one plug shape for every tool.
The LLM's request to do something, such as read_file("src/App.jsx"), which the agent then carries out.
The small chunk of text an LLM reads and writes; you're billed per token, both input and output.
The most tokens a model can consider at once, covering your whole conversation plus the files it read.
How hard Claude Code works before answering. Higher effort means more tool calls and more cost.
Reusing the already-sent part of a conversation at a big discount, which makes long sessions cheaper.
An open-source model running on your own computer: free, but weaker than Claude.

guide.title: Claude in Action
guide.summary: Run a real project through the Prompt Life Cycle (Define → Explore → Plan → Code → Review → Commit). Keep Claude's context small with CLAUDE.md and subagents, and have a QA subagent check your app in a real browser through the Playwright MCP.
guide.goal: Take one feature through the Prompt Life Cycle using plan mode, @-references, a project-mapper subagent and a Playwright-powered qa-agent.
required: Part I: Knowledge Check 5 – Prompt Life Cycle (team quiz)
Part I: Anthropic – Introduction to Subagents
Part I: FreeCodeCamp Python Certification – complete 50 steps
Part II: Knowledge Check 6 – More out of Claude Code (team quiz)
Part II: Anthropic – Claude 101
Part II: Anthropic – Claude Code 101
Part II: FreeCodeCamp JavaScript Certification – complete 100 steps

steps.title: Read the Prompt Life Cycle lecture
steps.detail: Learn the stages: Define (goal plus acceptance criteria), Explore (you find the relevant files), Plan (Claude plans in plan mode), Code, Review (a read-only subagent, ideally a stronger model), Document, Commit. The tic-tac-toe experiment shows why planning beats "Build a tic tac toe game".
steps.doneWhen: You can list the stages in order and say what you (not Claude) do in each one.

steps.title: Give each project a CLAUDE.md
steps.detail: Run /init in a project's root and Claude writes a CLAUDE.md that it reads first in every session; then edit it yourself. Know the three scopes: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (all your projects), CLAUDE.md (this project, committed) and .claude/CLAUDE.local.md (just you, not committed). Your netflix and hangman folders already have one.
steps.code:
/init
/context
steps.doneWhen: /context lists your CLAUDE.md under Memory Files.

steps.title: Document a project with project-mapper
steps.detail: A subagent works in its own context, so only its report lands in your main session. assignments/week-02/netflix/.claude/agents/project-mapper.md already exists. For any other project, create .claude/agents/project-mapper.md with the lecture's file, then run the lecture's prompt.
steps.code:
---
name: project-mapper
description: Scans files and generates a roadmap of documentation explaining where features are found within sections of files and how they connect to other pieces. Applying the Single Responsibility Principle to efficiently document a project.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
model: sonnet
---

You are Technical Lead in charge of this project. It is your task to scan through this codebase and return documentation explaining how the code base is laid out, how components speak to eachother, and create analogies that could be understood by team members with no technical background.

--- then, in Claude:
Write a README.md file along with a documentation directory holding the findings of the project-mapper agent.
steps.doneWhen: /agents lists project-mapper, and the project has a README.md plus a documentation folder written from its findings.

steps.title: Keep long sessions lean
steps.detail: Check usage with /context and /cost. The lecture's rule of thumb: /compact (summarize the history) at 60–70% full, and /clear or a new session above 80%. CLAUDE.md stays loaded after /clear.
steps.code:
/context
/cost
/compact
/clear
steps.doneWhen: You've watched the context bar drop after a /compact in a real session.

steps.title: Plan a feature in plan mode with @-files
steps.detail: Read your docs first to find the files a feature touches. Then press Shift+Tab until "plan" shows, and reference those files with @ so Claude doesn't search the whole codebase. Ask side questions with /btw so they don't clutter the main chat. Here is the lecture's prompt; write your own version for a Myflix feature.
steps.code:
I want to add a feature to this DBZ themed Tic Tac Toe game. Currently when someone wins the game they have to manually click `restart` in order to play the next game and there's no real signal that someone won the game.

I would like you to make it, where when a player wins the game a DBZ themed pop up in the center of the screen populates announcing the winner. Upon the modal closing the game should restart and be ready to start a new round.

From reading the documentation I believe you'll need to interact with these files:
- @index.html
- @script.js

Do you have any questions?
steps.doneWhen: Claude answered your questions in plan mode and saved a plan you approved before any code changed.

steps.title: Check the Playwright MCP is connected
steps.detail: Playwright lets Claude open a real browser, click and take screenshots. You already added it at user scope, so just confirm. The lecture's install command is below in case you ever need it on another machine. `claude -c` reopens your last session.
steps.code:
claude mcp add playwright npx @playwright/mcp@latest
claude -c
/mcp
steps.doneWhen: /mcp shows playwright as connected.

steps.title: Review your app with the qa-agent
steps.detail: The qa-agent (Opus, Playwright tools only) tests a feature list on desktop and mobile. assignments/week-02/netflix/.claude/agents/qa-agent.md already exists. Run the lecture's prompt in a project whose README lists its features, then play with the app yourself too.
steps.code:
I need to ensure this project is working well, open this project in a local browser. Once the project is open use the qa-agent by giving it the location of the project and the list of features from @README.md.

Once the agent comes back with it's findings update the code base and ensure to update the documentation to reflect the new state of the project.

Do you have any questions?
steps.doneWhen: The qa-agent's findings are fixed and the docs are updated, while your main session's context stays low.

steps.title: Take Knowledge Checks 5 and 6
steps.detail: KC5 (Prompt Life Cycle, CLAUDE.md scopes, subagents, /context /compact /clear) is done per progress.md. KC6 (plan mode, @ references, /btw, auto mode, Playwright MCP, the qa-agent) isn't forked yet. Run /start-assignment Knowledge-Check-6-More-out-of-Claude-Code, then take it with your team in Live Server.
steps.code: /start-assignment Knowledge-Check-6-More-out-of-Claude-Code
steps.doneWhen: KC6 is cloned under assignments/ (progress.md lists it in Week 2), and both quizzes are finished with your team.

steps.title: Anthropic courses and FreeCodeCamp
steps.detail: Part I: Introduction to Subagents plus 50 Python steps. Part II: Claude 101, Claude Code 101 plus 100 JavaScript steps. The page also suggests exploring the Claude Code docs as you go.
steps.doneWhen: All three Anthropic courses are complete and FreeCodeCamp shows the new steps.

Supabase's serverless functions. They run on Deno (a Node.js alternative) and live in supabase/functions/<name>/.
A browser rule: a page may only read a response from another origin if the server sends headers that allow it.
Protocol + domain + port, like http://localhost:5173. Change any one of them and it's a different origin.
The browser's "may I?" request before the real one. Your function must answer it with CORS headers.
Input in the URL (?a=6&b=6) vs input as JSON in a POST request.
Where a deployed function reads its keys, set with npx supabase secrets set and read with Deno.env.get.

Execute the following three phases in order. Do not begin a new phase until the current 
phase's completion criteria are met.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
PHASE 1 — SUPABASE AGENT
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Spawn a sub-agent scoped exclusively to the Supabase layer. This agent must not touch 
any front-end files.

This agent is responsible for:

1. Creating a new Supabase Edge Function named `process-donation` that:
   - Accepts a POST request with body: { amount: number (in cents), user_id: string }
   - Validates that the user is authenticated and the amount is a positive integer 
     greater than 0 and no greater than 1,000,000 (i.e. $10,000 max)
   - Uses STRIPE_SECRET_KEY from Supabase secrets (never hardcoded) to create a 
     Stripe Payment Intent
   - Returns: { client_secret: string }

2. Creating a `donations` table in the Supabase database with this schema:
   - id: uuid, primary key, default gen_random_uuid()
   - user_id: uuid, foreign key referencing auth.users
   - amount: integer (cents)
   - stripe_payment_intent_id: text, unique
   - status: text ('succeeded' or 'failed')
   - created_at: timestamptz, default now()

3. Creating a Row Level Security policy on `donations` such that:
   - Users can only SELECT their own rows (user_id = auth.uid())
   - No user can INSERT directly — inserts come only from the webhook handler
   - Service role can INSERT and UPDATE

4. Creating a new Supabase Edge Function named `stripe-webhook` that:
   - Listens for POST requests from Stripe
   - Validates the Stripe webhook signature using STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET from 
     Supabase secrets
   - Handles `payment_intent.succeeded`: checks if stripe_payment_intent_id already 
     exists in `donations` (idempotency), and if not, inserts a row with 
     status='succeeded'
   - Handles `payment_intent.payment_failed`: same idempotency check, inserts with 
     status='failed'
   - Returns 200 for all handled events, 400 for signature failures

Phase 1 is complete when:
- Both Edge Functions exist and are deployable without errors
- The `donations` table exists with the correct schema
- RLS policies are in place and correct
- No Stripe secret key appears in any committed file

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
PHASE 2 — UI AGENT
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Spawn a sub-agent scoped exclusively to the React + Vite front end. This agent must 
not touch any Supabase files, Edge Functions, or database migrations.

This agent is responsible for:

1. Creating a new React page component at the route `/donate` that:
   - Is registered in the existing React Router DOM setup
   - Displays a heading and brief description of the donation feature
   - Includes amount options (suggested: $5, $10, $25, $50) plus a custom amount 
     input
   - Embeds a Stripe Elements card input (CardElement) using @stripe/react-stripe-js
   - Has a "Donate" submit button

2. Implementing the payment flow in the donate page:
   - On submit, use the existing Axios instance to POST to the `process-donation` 
     Edge Function with: { amount: selectedAmountInCents, user_id: currentUser.id }
   - The current user's id is available from the existing auth context
   - On receiving { client_secret }, use Stripe.js (stripe.confirmCardPayment) — 
     NOT Axios — to confirm the Payment Intent directly with Stripe
   - Do not use Axios for the payment confirmation step

3. Rendering clear result states:
   - On success: display a thank-you message that includes the donation amount
   - On failure: display a user-friendly error message (no raw Stripe error codes 
     or stack traces visible to the user)
   - On network error (Edge Function unreachable): display a generic "something went 
     wrong" message and a retry option

4. Running Playwright verification after completing the UI. Use the existing 
   Playwright MCP setup to:
   - Navigate to /donate and confirm the page renders with the expected heading
   - Confirm the Stripe Elements iframe is present in the DOM
   - Select the $10 amount option
   - Complete the card input using Stripe test card: 4242 4242 4242 4242, 
     any future expiry, any CVC
   - Submit and confirm the success state renders
   - Reset and use decline card: 4000 0000 0000 0002
   - Submit and confirm the error state renders with a human-readable message

Phase 2 is complete when:
- The /donate route renders without errors
- The Stripe Elements card input is present and functional
- The Axios call targets the correct Edge Function endpoint
- Stripe.js (not Axios) is used for payment confirmation
- All Playwright verification steps pass

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
PHASE 3 — SUPERVISOR AGENT
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Spawn a sub-agent with read access to all files produced by Phase 1 and Phase 2. 
This agent must not write new feature code. It may only correct specific failures 
it identifies and document its findings.

This agent must first define its own passing requirements — before reviewing any 
code — based on what a correct, secure, production-ready Stripe one-time payment 
integration looks like. Document these requirements as a numbered list before 
proceeding.

Then review the output of both agents against those requirements, with explicit 
focus on:

1. API contract alignment: does the UI's Axios call body match exactly what the 
   `process-donation` Edge Function expects? Does it correctly consume 
   { client_secret } from the response?

2. Payment confirmation method: is stripe.confirmCardPayment (Stripe.js) being 
   used for the confirmation step — not a second Axios call?

3. Webhook registration: is the `stripe-webhook` Edge Function URL the one that 
   should be registered in the Stripe dashboard? Document the exact URL.

4. Idempotency: does the webhook handler check for an existing 
   stripe_payment_intent_id before inserting?

5. RLS correctness: can a user read another user's donation rows? Verify the 
   policy logic.

6. Security gate — CRITICAL: scan all front-end files for any occurrence of 
   STRIPE_SECRET_KEY or any string beginning with sk_. If found anywhere in 
   front-end code or committed environment files, this is a hard failure. 
   Report it immediately and halt.

After all checks pass, run the full Playwright suite one final time as an 
end-to-end integration verification.

Phase 3 output must include:
- The supervisor's self-defined passing requirements (numbered list)
- A pass/fail result for each check above
- The webhook URL to register in the Stripe dashboard
- The Playwright suite result (pass or specific failures)
- If any check failed: which agent is responsible and the exact correction needed

Phase 3 is complete when all checks pass and the final Playwright run succeeds.
steps.doneWhen: Phase 3 reports a pass/fail list, the webhook URL to register, and a Playwright result.

steps.title: Answer Claude's questions well
steps.detail: From the instructors' handoff notes: it's a Netflix clone, not a task manager, so donations live next to your lists. Use supabase.functions.invoke() (or the Axios you installed) instead of "the existing Axios instance". process-donation should take the user from the request's login token, not a user_id in the body (same idea as default auth.uid()). Deploy stripe-webhook with --no-verify-jwt: Stripe has no Supabase login and would get a 401. donations.user_id can point to auth.users or profiles (same ids); follow your list_entries table.
steps.doneWhen: Claude's plan uses the JWT for the user, and deploys stripe-webhook with --no-verify-jwt.

steps.title: Register the webhook, add its secret

npx supabase secrets set STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_YOUR_SIGNING_SECRET
npx supabase functions deploy stripe-webhook --no-verify-jwt
steps.doneWhen: The endpoint is listed in Stripe and npx supabase secrets list shows STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET.

steps.detail: Log in, open the Donate page, and pay $10 with 4242 4242 4242 4242 (any future date, any CVC). Then try the decline card 4000 0000 0000 0002: you should see a friendly error, not a code. The database should only change because of the webhook.

steps.title: Security check, then commit

git status
git add -A && git commit -m "Add Stripe one-time donation"
git push

concepts.meaning: A payments company. Your app never handles card numbers; it asks Stripe to charge them.
Stripe's record of one attempt to collect a payment, with a status like succeeded or requires_action.
A one-payment key your Edge Function gets from Stripe and hands to the browser so Stripe.js can confirm that payment.
Card input boxes hosted by Stripe inside your page (an iframe), so card data never touches your code.

guide.title: DevOps
guide.summary: What DevOps is (version control, CI/CD, monitoring) and a safe main / dev / feature branch workflow, then you put your app live: React front end on Vercel, Edge Functions and secrets on Supabase, and the Stripe webhook pointed at the live function.
guide.goal: Deploy Myflix to a public Vercel URL that logs in, loads data and takes a test donation, and ship later changes through feature → dev → main.
required: Part I: make sure your app(s) are ready for deployment and tied to Git or a cloud service: front end on GitHub, back end on Supabase
Part II: deploy your app(s), bring them live, and have something to demonstrate

steps.title: Make a dev branch
steps.detail: The lesson's workflow: main is what's live, dev collects finished work, and feature/* branches hold one change each. Myflix only has main. The instructors' notes say to create dev at the start of this lesson. Run this in ~/Desktop/codeplatoon/assignments/week-02/netflix.
steps.code:
git checkout main
git pull origin main
git checkout -b dev
git push -u origin dev
steps.doneWhen: github.com/cruzjay188/netflix shows both main and dev branches.

steps.title: Check main builds cleanly
steps.detail: The lecture's pre-deploy checklist (word for word below) uses client/; for you it's front-end/. If it doesn't build on your laptop, it won't build on Vercel. Merge dev into main first if dev is ahead.
steps.code:
# 1. Switch to main and pull the latest
git checkout main
git pull origin main

# 2. Verify the app builds cleanly (no errors)
cd client
npm run build

# 3. If you have a dev branch that's ahead of main, merge it
git checkout main
git merge dev
git push origin main
steps.doneWhen: npm run build in front-end/ finishes with no errors and makes a dist/ folder.

steps.title: Confirm no secrets are in Git
steps.detail: Part I: the front end lives on GitHub, the back end on Supabase, and keys live in neither repo. Only .env.example should match the search below. The lecture's rule: a VITE_ variable is bundled into the browser, so only public keys (Supabase publishable, Stripe pk_) go there.
steps.code:
git ls-files | grep -i env
grep -rn "sk_" front-end/src || echo "no secret keys"
steps.doneWhen: The first command lists only .env.example, and the second prints "no secret keys".

steps.title: Deploy Edge Functions and secrets
steps.detail: Vercel only deploys the front end. Edge Functions are a separate, manual deploy. Deploy every function in supabase/functions/ (tmdb, hello-world, process-donation, …). stripe-webhook needs --no-verify-jwt (instructors' notes). Then check the secrets (TMDB_API_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET) are set. SUPABASE_URL and the service-role key are injected for you.
steps.code:
npx supabase functions deploy
npx supabase functions deploy stripe-webhook --no-verify-jwt
npx supabase secrets list
steps.doneWhen: Supabase → Edge Functions lists every function, and secrets list shows your keys (names only).

steps.title: Import the repo into Vercel
steps.detail: vercel.com → Sign Up → Continue with GitHub → Add New Project → import cruzjay188/netflix. Set Root Directory to front-end (the lecture says client/). Framework Vite, build npm run build, output dist. Add environment variables with your names: VITE_SUPABASE_URL, VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY and VITE_STRIPE_PUBLIC_KEY. Then Deploy. If Myflix has URL routes by now, ask Claude for a front-end/vercel.json that rewrites every path to index.html (Ticked has one), so refreshing a deep link works.
steps.doneWhen: Vercel shows a successful deployment and https://<your-app>.vercel.app opens Myflix.

steps.title: Tell Supabase Auth your live URL
steps.detail: From the instructors' notes, after the first Vercel deploy: Supabase → Authentication → URL Configuration. Set the Site URL to your Vercel URL, and add it plus http://localhost:5173 to Redirect URLs. Otherwise auth links point at localhost.
steps.doneWhen: URL Configuration shows the Vercel URL as Site URL, with both URLs in Redirect URLs.

steps.title: Test the whole flow live
steps.detail: Lecture step 5: on the Vercel URL, sign up / log in, use the app, go to Donate, and pay with 4242 4242 4242 4242. The Stripe webhook already points at your Supabase function, which is the same URL in production. The lecture's slides switch to sk_live_/pk_live_ keys, but 4242 only works in test mode. Stay on test keys unless the instructors say otherwise (ask in #eagle_questions).
steps.doneWhen: A new row appears in Table Editor → donations, and you have a live link to demo.

steps.title: Know where to look when it breaks
steps.detail: After every deploy, check the lecture's three places: Vercel → Deployments (did the build pass?), Supabase → Edge Functions → Logs (errors?), Stripe → Developers → Webhooks (200 responses?). To roll back, use Vercel's Promote to Production on an older deployment.
steps.doneWhen: You've opened all three dashboards and seen a green build, clean logs, and 200s.

steps.title: Ship one change the safe way
steps.detail: The golden rule: never push straight to main. Make a small change on a feature branch, open a PR into dev (Vercel builds a preview URL for it), merge, then open a PR from dev to main to go live. Log the live URL in progress.md and in the Netflix project hub.
steps.code:
git checkout dev
git checkout -b feature/small-change
# make the change with Claude, then:
git add -A && git commit -m "feat: small change"
git push -u origin feature/small-change
# on GitHub: PR feature/small-change → dev, then PR dev → main
steps.doneWhen: The PR shows a Vercel preview link, and after merging dev → main the live site shows the change.

concepts.meaning: Building and running software as one team, with automation for testing, deploying and watching it.
Every push is tested and built automatically, so broken code is caught early.
Code that passes is deployed automatically. Here, a push to main makes Vercel redeploy.
main = live, dev = tested work waiting to ship, feature/* = one change in progress.
A host for front-end apps. It builds your React app from GitHub and serves it on HTTPS.
A temporary live URL Vercel makes for each pull request, so you can test before merging.
A setting stored outside the code (Vercel dashboard, Supabase secrets) instead of committed to Git.
Putting an older working version back live (Vercel: Promote to Production).

guide.title: Github Actions
guide.summary: GitHub Actions runs checks for you every time code changes: workflows written in YAML, triggered by events (push, pull request, manual), made of jobs and steps, with logs in the Actions tab. It's the CI part of DevOps. The step-by-step arrives when the lecture is published.

steps.title: Read a workflow file
steps.detail: Workflows live in .github/workflows/*.yml. This minimal one matches the curriculum's Hello Workflows idea: run on every push to any branch, on Ubuntu, and echo a message. Don't commit it anywhere yet. Just read it and look up any line you don't know.
steps.code:
name: Hello Workflows
on:
  push:

guide.summary: Introduces divide and conquer: split a problem into smaller copies of itself, solve them, then combine the results. Merge Sort is the example: split the list into single items, then merge sorted pieces back together, for O(n log n) time. The lesson shows an iterative version and says the recursive version comes later. Step-by-step guide arrives when the lecture is published.

steps.title: Run the merge step on its own
steps.detail: merge() is the heart of Merge Sort. Copy it from the lesson and run it on two sorted lists.
steps.code:
def merge(left, right):
    result = []
    i, j = 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] < right[j]:
            result.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result

print(merge([1, 4, 5], [2, 3, 6]))

guide.summary: Covers the two main ways to walk a tree. Depth First Search (DFS) goes as deep as possible down one branch before backing up, and fits naturally with recursion. Breadth First Search (BFS) visits the tree level by level using a queue, and finds the shortest path in an unweighted tree. Step-by-step guide arrives when the lecture is published.
guide.goal: Write DFS and BFS traversals for a binary tree and choose the right one for a problem.

steps.title: Read the lesson

steps.title: Try pre-order and post-order
steps.detail: Move the print in dfs_in_order before the left call (pre-order), then after the right call (post-order), and compare the outputs.
steps.doneWhen: You can predict the order for each version before running it.

steps.title: Talk through the two assignments
steps.detail: The assignments are Maximum Depth of a Binary Tree and Level Order Traversal. For each, say out loud which traversal you'd use and why, then its Big-O (both are O(n) time; DFS space is O(h), BFS space is O(w) for the widest level).

concepts.meaning: Visiting every node in a structure in a set order.

Left, node, right; on a BST it gives values in sorted order.
